opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't say it will necessarily backfire for everybody, but there is a pattern that history keeps repeating, and many people seem to forget it.

For many decades, compute has become cheaper by roughly a factor of 100 per decade. So whatever you buy today at enormous cost, a few years from now somebody will be able to get the same capability for a small fraction of the price. If you build a gigantic data center now, you are betting that your head start matters more than the depreciation of your hardware, and hardware depreciates very fast.

The second point is that the methods change. Much of today's infrastructure is optimized for one particular way of doing things: very large Transformer-like models trained on huge amounts of passive data. But that is not the end of AI history. The next big wave is likely to be about AIs that learn more like little scientists or babies, building world models, running experiments, inventing their own goals, learning from their own actions rather than just imitating text from the internet. If that kind of learning turns out to be much more data-efficient and compute-efficient, then a lot of the specialized infrastructure built for brute-force scaling may suddenly look oversized.

Third, there is the question of moats. Again and again we have seen that once something is shown to be possible, others replicate it quickly and more cheaply, often with open-source models. So a company may invest tens of billions, and then a small lab somewhere reproduces most of the value for a tiny fraction of that. This has happened before and will happen again.

So the risk is not that AI is overhyped in the long run. In the long run, AI will be much more important than most people think. The risk is that specific bets on today's hardware and today's methods, at today's prices, may not pay off the way investors expect. The future belongs to whoever keeps up with the exponential, not to whoever has spent the most on one snapshot of it.

r001.rationale: It says compute gets roughly 100 times cheaper per decade, so the same capability can soon be obtained for a small fraction of today’s cost.

r002.rationale: It says companies are betting that their head start will matter more than rapid hardware depreciation, identifying competitive advantage as a reason to invest now.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute to large companies an expectation that achieving true AGI would be worth vastly more than their computing investment.

r004.rationale: It links the risk to fast depreciation, changing methods, and replication; it does not say investments may backfire because they are made before computers are fast enough.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, I should say I don't think they will backfire in the sense that the compute will be useless. Compute is never wasted for long. But I think the current investments are based on a misunderstanding of where progress actually comes from, and that misunderstanding is expensive.

Look at the history. Every five years, compute gets roughly ten times cheaper. This has been true for about 80 years, since Konrad Zuse built the first working program-controlled computer in 1941. So if you spend, say, 50 billion dollars today on a data center, in five years the same capability costs 5 billion, and in ten years half a billion. Whoever waits gets the same thing for a fraction of the price. The first mover pays a huge premium, and the premium only pays off if the first mover gets something durable in return. And what is durable here? Not the hardware, which depreciates very quickly. Not the models, because everybody is training essentially the same architectures on essentially the same data, and the results converge. The large language models of different companies are becoming interchangeable commodities. You can see it in the prices, which fall toward zero.

The second thing is that the industry is currently obsessed with scaling one particular idea, which is a transformer trained to predict the next token. Many of the basic principles behind this are old, by the way. The unnormalized linear transformer, what is now called linear attention, we published in 1991, and it was essentially a neural network that learns to program the fast weights of another neural network. And these companies are now spending hundreds of billions to scale up variants of this. But scaling a fixed idea has diminishing returns, as everybody is now noticing. The real breakthroughs historically came from algorithmic insights, not from brute force. Backpropagation, LSTM, the GAN principle which we called artificial curiosity in 1990, all of these were invented by very small groups with very little compute. Then the hardware caught up and made them practical. The idea came first, the compute came later. Now people are trying to reverse this order, and buy their way to the next idea with GPUs. That has never worked before.

And there is a third point, which is that the next step, the really important step, is not going to be a bigger passive model that answers questions. It will be active agents that learn by interacting with the world, that set their own goals, that have intrinsic motivation, curiosity, and that build models of the world through experience. This is what we have been working on since the early 1990s. Such systems don't necessarily need these enormous centralized training runs. A curious little robot does not need a gigawatt data center. It needs good algorithms. So companies that build their entire strategy around enormous centralized compute for pretraining are optimizing for the current paradigm precisely at the moment when it is about to be replaced.

So my prediction is this: the hardware will eventually be used for something, of course. But much of the value will be captured not by those who bought it, but by those who come later with better ideas, running on hardware that is ten or a hundred times cheaper. That's what I mean by backfire. It's not a catastrophe, it's just history repeating itself, as it always does in this field.

r001.rationale: The response says compute gets roughly ten times cheaper every five years and gives examples of the same data-center capability costing much less if purchased later.

r002.rationale: It discusses first movers paying a premium and needing durable returns, but does not identify competitive pressure as the reason companies are investing now.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute to large companies an expectation that achieving AGI would be worth vastly more than their computing investment.

r004.rationale: It says companies are investing before better algorithmic ideas and while scaling a fixed approach has diminishing returns; it does not say they are investing before computers are fast enough.

astra-6.text:
I think the risk is that they are extrapolating today’s computational requirements into the future. They assume that better AI will require ever larger models and ever more computing infrastructure. But that ignores improvements in algorithms. A more efficient method can make a task that was enormously expensive suddenly quite cheap.

Now, if you have committed billions to infrastructure on the assumption that the current approach will remain dominant, that is a dangerous situation. Your competitor may achieve comparable results with much less computation, while you still have to pay for your investment.

Of course, cheaper computation can also create more demand. So I would not say that all these investments must fail. But there is a big difference between believing that AI will become tremendously important and believing that today’s enormous infrastructure investments will earn an adequate return.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithms may make tasks cheaper, but does not explain that delaying computation as computers get cheaper would reduce the cost of doing the same work.

r002.rationale: It mentions competitors achieving comparable results with less computation, but does not identify competitive pressure as a reason companies invest now despite potential savings from waiting.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention AGI or attribute to companies an expectation that its value would vastly exceed their computing investment.

r004.rationale: It links risk to committing billions on the assumption that current approaches will remain dominant, but does not attribute backfiring to investing before computers are fast enough.

sol-6.1.text:
Because they are betting that the enormous computational cost of today’s AI will persist. But AI is becoming more efficient through better algorithms as well as better hardware. If you build a huge, expensive computing center today, a competitor may soon accomplish the same thing with a much smaller investment. Your facility may still work, but economically it may no longer be competitive.

There is also a difference between AI becoming enormously useful and the companies supplying it earning enormous profits. Competition can make intelligence cheaper and cheaper. That is wonderful for users, but it can be a problem for companies that have spent vast sums assuming they will be able to charge high prices.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithms and hardware are making AI more efficient, but it does not clearly state that delaying the same computation would substantially reduce its cost.

r002.rationale: It mentions that a competitor may achieve the same result with less investment, but does not explain competitive pressure as a reason companies invest now despite savings from waiting.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute to the companies an expectation that achieving true AGI would be worth vastly more than their computing investment.

r004.rationale: It attributes the risk to costs falling and companies expecting high prices, not to investing before computers are fast enough.
